strengths: The paper targets a timely and underexplored problem: evaluating mobile agents that combine flexible GUI interaction with APIs, deep links, and reusable automation scripts. This is relevant to language-guided agent planning and execution.

MAS-Bench has meaningful scope: 139 tasks across 11 applications, including both single-app and cross-app workflows, together with 88 shortcuts of several types. The hybrid action taxonomy and evaluation dimensions are clearly motivated.

The paired T3A/MAS-T3A and MobileAgentV2/MAS-MobileAgent comparisons provide useful preliminary evidence that predefined shortcuts can improve success and efficiency across UI-tree and screenshot-based agents. Experiments with two Gemini model variants further suggest that weaker agents benefit more.

The paper does not hide negative results: generated shortcuts are often unreliable, and the failure analysis identifies shortcut-selection, adaptation, and formulation errors. These observations could help guide future work.
weaknesses: The benchmark is not currently reproducible. The stated project-page URL is missing, and the manuscript does not provide the promised task list, task success predicates, shortcut implementations, prompts, retrieval procedure, application versions, account/data setup, environment-reset protocol, model parameters, or complete evaluator details. Live proprietary applications and Gemini models make these omissions especially consequential.

The shortcut-generation experiment appears to generate shortcuts from trajectories for the same 69-task subset on which those shortcuts are subsequently evaluated. Without disjoint generation and evaluation tasks—or preferably held-out applications—this primarily measures task-specific replay or memorization rather than reusable abstraction and generalization. The random subset seed and shortcut-selection protocol are also unspecified.

The experimental evidence lacks repeated trials, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests, despite claims of significant improvements. Mobile interaction and proprietary LLM inference are stochastic, while live applications introduce additional variation; apparent differences based on what seems to be one execution per task may therefore be unstable.

Success evaluation is underspecified. The paper only says that it adapts SPA-Bench and embeds shortcut descriptions, without defining executable goal predicates or validating automatic judgments against human annotations. Consequently, the primary success-rate results cannot be independently audited.

The benchmark is constructed so that every task has at least one hand-designed applicable shortcut, making improvement from the curated knowledge base partly built into the task design. This establishes that task-specific shortcuts can help, but does not yet demonstrate robust shortcut discovery, optimal GUI-versus-shortcut decision-making, or generalization to naturally occurring tasks.

Several efficiency metrics are difficult to interpret fairly. MSRS conditions on successful runs and is vulnerable to survivor bias; the source of the claimed optimal step count is unclear; execution time is confounded by framework and service latency; and token accounting is not defined. GSAR is also described inconsistently: a higher GUI-to-shortcut ratio does not itself demonstrate greater shortcut use or efficiency.

The baseline comparison is incomplete and sometimes confounded by differences in agent architecture and input modality. Although the paired ablations are more informative, the paper does not isolate gains from shortcut availability versus retrieval context, prompts, or other MAS integration changes.

The broad claims of being the first unified benchmark and of framework-agnostic effectiveness are stronger than the presented evidence. The related-benchmark comparison uses coarse binary judgments, and validation covers only two adapted architectures, a single primary model family, one emulator configuration, and 11 task-selected applications.

Overall, the direction is promising, but the missing release-level specification, lack of rigorous repeated evaluation, and leakage in the shortcut-generation study prevent a sound and reproducible Findings recommendation in the current form. These issues appear addressable in a substantial next-cycle revision.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: mobile GUI agents can benefit from combining flexible interaction with APIs, deep links, and reusable automation routines.
MAS-Bench has potentially useful breadth, covering 139 tasks, 11 applications, single- and cross-application workflows, and several shortcut types.

The paired comparisons between T3A and MAS-T3A and between MobileAgentV2 and MAS-MobileAgent suggest that curated shortcuts can improve success and efficiency across both UI-tree and screenshot-based agents.
The paper reports multiple operational metrics and includes illustrative failure cases that expose shortcut-selection, adaptation, and formulation errors.
weaknesses: The central benchmark is not reproducible from the manuscript. The promised task list is absent, the project-page URL is blank, application versions and complete shortcut definitions are not reported, and prompts, retrieval details, evaluator configuration, execution settings, and environment-reset procedures are insufficiently specified.

The success evaluation lacks validation. The paper only states that an automated method adapted from SPA-Bench embeds shortcut descriptions to determine success or failure; it provides no precise decision procedure, evaluator agreement with human judgments, error analysis, or task-specific checks. Consequently, the reliability of the primary SR results is unknown.

The shortcut-generation experiment appears to generate shortcuts from task instructions and execution histories and then evaluate them on the same 69-task subset. Without a disjoint generation/evaluation split, the experiment measures reuse or memorization on seen workflows rather than transferable shortcut generation. The generated knowledge bases also contain different numbers of shortcuts, further confounding comparison.

The claim of an unbiased shortcut-quality evaluation is unsupported. Performance after importing a knowledge base into T3A depends jointly on shortcut coverage, representation, retrieval, argument grounding, and T3A's selection behavior; these factors are neither isolated nor controlled.

The paper reports single aggregate results without repeated trials, confidence intervals, significance tests, seeds, or analysis of API/model nondeterminism, despite repeatedly describing improvements as significant. This is especially problematic for an online benchmark involving stochastic LLMs and changing real-world applications.

Several metrics are unclear or internally inconsistent. GSAR is defined as GUI actions divided by shortcut actions, yet GUI-only systems are assigned zero rather than an undefined or infinite value, and a higher value is interpreted as stronger shortcut utilization. MSRS is computed only over successful tasks, so comparisons are selection-biased when systems succeed on different task subsets.

The benchmark is deliberately constructed so every task has an applicable curated shortcut, and the reported predefined shortcuts have 100% execution success. This supports the unsurprising claim that reliable, task-aligned automation helps, but it does not establish robustness under irrelevant, incomplete, ambiguous, stale, or failing shortcut libraries—the conditions most important to the broader claim.

Efficiency comparisons are incomplete and sometimes misleading: execution time may depend on model latency and external services; token totals are unusually large but unexplained; shortcut construction and retrieval costs are omitted; and no end-to-end cost of generating shortcuts is included.

The benchmark's broader validity is weakly established. Task creation methodology, annotator involvement, optimal-step calculation, realism, contamination risks, and task coverage are not documented sufficiently, while comparisons with prior benchmarks are reduced to coarse checkmarks.

These issues affect the soundness of the main benchmark and generation claims rather than presentation alone. Addressing them would require releasing complete artifacts, validating the evaluator, redesigning the shortcut-generation split and controls, and rerunning experiments with uncertainty estimates, which is substantial work unlikely to fit within one review cycle.

strengths: The paper targets an important and relatively underexplored problem: evaluating mobile agents that combine flexible GUI interaction with APIs, deep links, and reusable automation scripts. This is relevant to increasingly tool-oriented LLM agents.

MAS-Bench has meaningful breadth, with 139 tasks across 11 applications, including 47 cross-application tasks, 88 predefined shortcuts, multiple shortcut-generation strategies, and metrics covering task success, execution effort, latency, token use, and shortcut behavior.

The paired comparisons are informative: adding the same shortcut mechanism to MobileAgentV2 and T3A generally improves success and efficiency, including large gains on difficult cross-application tasks. Testing both screenshot- and UI-tree-based agents provides some evidence that the approach transfers across perception modalities.

The shortcut-generation study yields a useful negative result: generated shortcuts remain substantially less robust than manually defined ones. The breakdown among task replay, subtask replay, dynamic grounding, and MobileAgent-E shortcuts helps expose distinct limitations.
The paper is clearly organized, visually polished, and includes concrete workflow illustrations, model-capability comparisons, difficulty-stratified results, and qualitative failure analysis.
weaknesses: The benchmark is not presently reproducible from the paper. The project-page URL is blank, the promised task list is absent, and exact task specifications, train/test identities and random seed, app versions, prompts, shortcut implementations, retrieval procedure, emulator reset protocol, and full evaluator implementation are not provided. Dynamic real-world applications make these omissions especially consequential.

The validity of the automatic success evaluation is insufficiently established. The paper only states that it adapts SPA-Bench and embeds shortcut-action descriptions; it does not define the decision procedure or report agreement with independent human judgments, false-positive/negative rates, or robustness across application states. Since success rate is the central outcome, evaluator validation is essential.

The experiments report point estimates from apparently one run per task, without repeated trials, uncertainty intervals, or significance tests. LLM decisions, online application state, latency, and external content are stochastic, so claims of significant improvements and fine-grained differences between methods are unsupported statistically.

The shortcut-generation evaluation appears to generate shortcuts from trajectories for the same 69-task subset on which the resulting knowledge bases are evaluated. This permits task-specific memorization—particularly for task-level replay—and does not establish reusable shortcut discovery or generalization to held-out tasks. Knowledge bases also differ in size and likely coverage, confounding generation quality with availability.

The benchmark construction favors the proposed intervention: every task is selected to have an applicable predefined shortcut, and the manually authored shortcuts reportedly execute with 100% success. The results therefore show that privileged, reliable actions can help on shortcut-compatible tasks, but provide weaker evidence that MAS-Bench measures general intelligent discovery or optimal GUI-versus-shortcut selection. Evaluation on held-out tasks without guaranteed shortcut utility and controlled oracle/retrieval baselines would strengthen this claim.

Several efficiency metrics need clearer definitions and less biased analysis. MSRS and execution time appear conditioned on successful tasks, meaning methods are compared on different task subsets; the optimal-step reference is not explained; and GSAR is assigned a higher-is-better direction even though a high GUI-to-shortcut ratio does not itself demonstrate efficient shortcut use. Cost reporting also omits shortcut construction and retrieval overhead.

The claims that the benefits are framework-agnostic and that this is the first systematic benchmark are broader than the evidence supports. Only two closely related agent adaptations are tested, while the related-work comparison uses coarse checkmarks and does not carefully delimit the contribution against recent self-evolving skill and hybrid GUI/API benchmarks.

Overall, the idea and initial evidence are promising, but evaluator validation, held-out shortcut-generation experiments, uncertainty estimates, and a complete reproducibility package are needed before the work clearly meets the soundness and reproducibility threshold for Findings.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: evaluating mobile agents that combine GUI interaction with APIs, deep links, and RPA-style shortcuts. The distinction between shortcut selection and shortcut generation is useful.

MAS-Bench has meaningful breadth: 139 single- and cross-app tasks across 11 applications, 88 predefined shortcuts of several types, multiple agent architectures and model families, and metrics covering success, steps, latency, token use, and shortcut behavior.

Matched GUI-only versus shortcut-augmented comparisons provide substantial evidence that reliable shortcuts can improve task success and efficiency. The cross-app breakdown and irrelevant-shortcut interference experiment are particularly informative.

The authors validate the automated evaluator on 278 human-labeled trajectories and report strong precision, recall, and F1. Snapshot restoration, isolated test accounts, and emulator specifications are also sensible controls.
The paper openly reports negative results: some models misuse shortcuts, ScaleCUA variants obtain little or negative benefit, and most generated shortcuts do not improve both success and efficiency.
weaknesses: The benchmark is not currently reproducible from the manuscript. The project-page field is blank, and the paper does not provide the tasks, task-level initial states, complete shortcut implementations, prompts, evaluation code, application versions, model decoding settings, or emulator image. This is a decisive issue for a benchmark contribution.

The shortcut-generation experiment appears to generate shortcuts from trajectories for the same randomly selected 69 tasks on which their quality is subsequently evaluated. No held-out tasks, applications, or temporal/UI variants are described. This permits task-specific memorization and does not support claims about learning reusable shortcuts or generalizing from interaction.

Results appear to come from one execution per task, with no repeated trials, confidence intervals, significance tests, or analysis of model/API nondeterminism. Consequently, claims that gains are significant and fine-grained comparisons between methods are not statistically justified.

Several comparisons are confounded by giving augmented agents an extra, manually curated and task-aligned action space. Application-name filtering ensures relevant shortcuts remain available, and each complex shortcut counts as one step regardless of its internal work. The experiments establish utility of this particular curated tool interface, but less clearly an agent's autonomous shortcut-discovery capability or intrinsic planning improvement.

The automated-evaluation validation lacks sufficient annotation detail: the number of annotators, adjudication process, inter-annotator agreement, class balance, sampling procedure, and uncertainty are absent. It also relies on proprietary Gemini models, further limiting reproducibility. Calling 278 trajectories “tasks” is confusing because this exceeds the benchmark's 139 tasks.

There are internal reporting inconsistencies, including different cross-app execution times for MAS-MobileAgent in Tables 5 and 10. The broad “framework-agnostic” conclusion is also too strong given the negligible or negative results for several specialized GUI models.

Dynamic online applications and dedicated accounts make long-term replication difficult. Snapshot restoration controls device state but does not freeze server-side content, recommendation state, application updates, or service behavior; the paper does not quantify residual variation.

The novelty claim of being the first unified benchmark needs more careful positioning against prior hybrid GUI/API and self-evolving-agent evaluations. The contribution is promising, but the present evidence and missing artifacts prevent a sound, reproducible Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: evaluating mobile agents that combine GUI interaction with APIs, deep links, and RPA-style shortcuts.

MAS-Bench has meaningful breadth, with 139 tasks across 11 applications, 88 predefined shortcuts, single- and cross-application workflows, and experiments covering several agent architectures and model families.

Paired GUI-only versus shortcut-augmented comparisons generally support the limited claim that curated shortcuts can improve success and wall-clock efficiency in this environment. The negative ScaleCUA and Qwen results also usefully show that shortcut exposure is not universally beneficial.

The paper considers more than task success: it reports execution time, steps, token use, shortcut-selection quality, irrelevant-shortcut interference, and failure cases. The automated evaluator is also checked against 278 human-labeled trajectories and achieves over 95% F1.
weaknesses: The main evaluation is structurally favorable to the proposed paradigm. Every benchmark task is deliberately designed to have a relevant predefined shortcut, and application names are extracted from instructions to expose only shortcuts for those applications. This controlled, nearly oracle retrieval setting does not substantiate broad claims about autonomous shortcut discovery or reliable selection from realistic, large tool spaces. The distractor experiment is limited to a selected set of 23 cross-app tasks and five models.

The shortcut-generation evaluation has a serious potential leakage problem. The manuscript does not establish a disjoint split between trajectories used to generate shortcuts and tasks used to evaluate their reuse; both stages appear to operate on the same 69-task subset. Consequently, the results do not demonstrate abstraction or generalization to unseen tasks. Only one generator configuration is studied, generation costs are omitted, and the compared shortcut types differ substantially in runtime capabilities.

Efficiency is partly built into the metric definition: an API, deep link, or RPA workflow containing many internal operations counts as one step and is compared with a pure-GUI human baseline. Thus sub-1.0 step ratios are largely expected rather than evidence of superior planning. Wall-clock and token measurements are more informative, but the paper provides no repeated trials or uncertainty estimates for these noisy quantities.

The experiments appear to use one stochastic trajectory per task. There are no multiple runs, confidence intervals, significance tests, or robustness analysis across model sampling and dynamic online content. Claims that improvements are significant are therefore unsupported, and several reported differences are only one or a few successful tasks.

Reproducibility is inadequate for Findings in its present form. The project-page field is blank, and the submission does not provide the task instances, shortcut implementations, prompts, exact application versions, model decoding settings, action budgets, evaluator prompts, snapshot image, or runnable code. Dedicated online accounts and changing proprietary applications further complicate independent replication.

The evaluator validation is useful but incomplete: all evaluated trajectories come from one agent family, the human-annotation protocol and inter-annotator agreement are not reported, and uncertainty or confusion counts are absent. This does not establish reliability across the diverse agents whose outputs are scored.

The claimed stability of all 88 shortcuts across at least five application versions is asserted without listing versions, dates, per-shortcut outcomes, or a reproducible test protocol. Likewise, the benchmark's task quality and shortcut annotations receive no independent validation or agreement analysis.

Overall, the benchmark idea is promising, but the evidence currently supports only the narrower conclusion that task-aligned, human-curated shortcuts help selected agents on a benchmark constructed around those shortcuts. A clear release, statistically rigorous reruns, realistic retrieval evaluation, and leakage-free shortcut-generation split are important revisions that could reasonably support resubmission next cycle.

strengths: The paper introduces a timely and relevant benchmark for hybrid mobile agents that combine language-model-driven GUI interaction with APIs, deep links, and RPA scripts. Evaluating both shortcut selection and shortcut generation is a useful extension beyond existing mobile-agent benchmarks.

The benchmark has meaningful breadth: 139 tasks across 11 real applications, 88 predefined shortcuts, single- and cross-application workflows, multiple difficulty levels, and nine metrics covering success, efficiency, and resource use.

The empirical evaluation is unusually extensive, spanning agentic workflows, general-purpose vision-language models, specialized GUI models, two perception modalities, and multiple model scales. Matched GUI-only versus hybrid comparisons generally support the central claim that reliable shortcuts can improve success and efficiency.

The paper does not report only favorable cases. Results for weaker and specialized models show that shortcuts can be redundant or harmful, and the irrelevant-shortcut experiment directly tests misuse. Shortcut-selection precision, recall, redundancy, and failure analyses make the benchmark more diagnostically useful.

The shortcut-generation study controls the executor by importing each generated knowledge base into the same baseline agent. Its negative findings are informative: automatically generated shortcuts remain substantially less robust than carefully constructed structural shortcuts.

The automated evaluator is checked against 278 manually labeled trajectories and attains over 95% F1 for both single- and cross-app tasks. The snapshot-reset mechanism, isolated accounts, human step baselines, and testing of shortcuts across application versions are additional methodological strengths.
The presentation is clear and well organized, with readable tables, concrete shortcut examples, task breakdowns, and explicit limitations.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not yet demonstrated at the level expected of a benchmark contribution. The manuscript provides no usable project link or explicit artifact-release commitment, and does not enumerate the 139 task instructions, evaluator prompts, agent prompts, exact application versions, shortcut implementations, or test-account setup. A snapshot cannot fully stabilize externally hosted content or future application behavior.

The reported agent results appear to come from a single execution per task. There are no repeated trials, confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or variance estimates despite stochastic models and dynamic online applications. Consequently, the reliability of smaller gains—and some conclusions comparing models—is unclear.

The shortcut-generation experiment appears to generate and evaluate shortcuts on the same randomly selected 69-task subset, without a reported random seed or a held-out split by task pattern. Because many tasks are incremental variants, this setup can reward task-specific replay or leakage rather than demonstrate reusable shortcut abstraction and generalization to unseen workflows.

The predefined knowledge base is manually curated so that every task has at least one usable shortcut. Improvements therefore establish the benefit of privileged, task-relevant tools more directly than agents' ability to discover useful shortcuts in realistic, large, incomplete, or changing tool pools. The 23-task distractor experiment helps, but is small and removes all relevant tools rather than evaluating retrieval from a genuinely large mixed pool.

The automated evaluator validation uses trajectories from only MAS-MobileAgent. The paper does not report the number of human annotators, adjudication procedure, inter-annotator agreement, label balance, or performance across other agent families and failure modes. Gemini-based agents are also partly judged by Gemini models, creating a potential shared-model bias that is not examined.

Some efficiency metrics need more careful interpretation. Counting an entire RPA workflow as one step makes step reduction partly definitional, while higher shortcut-call count and shortcut-to-GUI ratio are marked as intrinsically desirable even though the paper itself shows that excessive calls can be harmful. Wall-clock time and token results mitigate this issue but also lack uncertainty estimates.

The claim of being the first unified benchmark is plausible but stronger than the comparison establishes, and statements such as guaranteeing 'absolute environment consistency' overstate what snapshot restoration can provide when online services remain dynamic. These limitations keep the work just below a confident main-conference recommendation, although the core benchmark and evidence appear suitable for Findings.
